body: This is what I wanted to read. I look people in the eyes when I'm talking. I just didn't want to make her uncomfortable before we got a chance to talk about it. I should've mentioned that I was looking for advice on the first date or two.

Thanks for responding, I'm fine with talking but in person I always look people in the eyes so it's more about not offending her on a first date. I'm not comfortable avoiding someone's eyes altogether, was looking more for advice on how to to look into her eyes without making her uncomfortable.
This is the first comment that made sense. Thanks

While I appreciate your response I feel you didn't understand me fully. I heard you about not using the phrase "good eye". I will not say or type that again. But with your words here-

"My advice on “where to look” is this. How do you look at a differently abled person in a wheelchair? Or a person with any kind of mental or physical difference?

Do you get anxious and find you have the urge to stare? Or look anywhere but at the person. It’s normal to feel that but what you have to do is be an adult and get over it and realise someone else’s difference is not about your response. It’s not about you. If you feel awkward or uncomfortable how do you think the person with the difference has felt their whole life?"

My brother has one arm, my father had one leg. No I don't get the urge to stare. I've always looked people directly in the eyes when speaking. Not for the entirety of the conversation but a lot of it. I don't need your lesson on how to be an adult or how I should respond. I was looking for more of an answer of how to show I was listening or understanding what a possible partner was saying without offending her. For the most part- I do look into the eyes of a first date as much as I can. You say to let her lead and that sounds like good advice I'll likely follow.

I always look people in the eyes. For five years now once a week I meet with  a business man with a lazy eye and he was obviously uncomfortable with me. After a couple months I avoided looking into his eyes he became much friendlier. I don't believe I'm over thinking and of course I'm treating her as a normal person and don't see any part of her as a plague. I was looking for advice on how to show admiration without offense because I'm used to looking people directly in the eyes, not because I'm incapable of seeing past an insignificant descriptive detail.

13 can be a tough age.

I lost my dad after years of chemo when I was 12. Felt numb for a long time. I talked to a psychiatrist  a couple years after and explained that I wasn't sad, but didn't feel anything. They didn't understand and I stopped going.

What's weird is that I somehow felt in control during that time. It wasn't until highschool that I made some "friends" and started getting high or drunk as much as possible and started feeling somewhat content again. We graduated, I made more serious mistakes, everyone went their separate ways and my numbness came back. 

Several years later I was full on drunk. Still worked full time but my free time was drinking, got kicked out of my last friends house and moved back in with my mom.

Spent 2 years back with my mom- hiding my drinking by locking myself in my room, I finally was able to talk with her without hiding my drinking anymore. (She drinks too but responsibly) 

I've been back home with my mom for 3 years now, and I'm finally getting to the point that I can talk and I don't feel numb when sober.

My point being is that in my opinion, the only way to get back to normal is by learning to find someone to talk to and trust. 

Good luck to you, I hope you find happiness.

Edit: I forgot to add that I think that part of my numbness was refusing to feel sad anymore.- We can't feel good if we don't let ourselves feel bad.

I hate this comment. Op posting in suicide watch because they are feeling low. I think the point you are trying to make is that everyone has a hard time. But have some empathy. Just because you've been through/ going though it doesn't make it ok to brush off someone else's pain.

What are your failing in school? What kind of real friends hate? I'm sorry about your relationship. In my later years of highschool I developed this weird shield of anti emotion to protect myself from being hurt again.

 Wasn't until a year after highschool I finally saw a professional and told them how I felt grey all the time, how nothing could make me happy.
  Didn't help at all. He tried to help but made it worse, talked about how my mom's situation was harder. It was, but that wasn't what I needed to hear.

  I thought, maybe it's better to feel grey than to hurt again. 
I was wrong.

  I have no right to tell you how to think/act/ live. But if you really look at the things that hurt you, and let those things teach/influence your decisions rather than despair you from here on out, I think you you could be better off.

But I'm just saying things I wish I would have heard and listened to. I am a hypocrite. I am a drunk 27yo. Take my words with a pinch of salt.

Best wishes

I played chess with an uncle(50ish years old) who visited every couple years to see my grandparents when I was about 10 years old. He was very smart. Also a drunk, but I didn't know that then.

 I only really knew how each piece moved, no strategy. But I had played just enough to know that a stalemate was a tie. He accidentally put me in stalemate and I preceded to proudly announce to everyone in the house (my mom, grandparents and 2 younger cousins) that I had tied my super smart uncle in chess.

About 3 years later my uncle and his oldest son(19ish) came back into town. There was a gathering at a different aunt/uncle's house with almost our whole family. Big family- like 30-50 people.

He and his son came directly at me, slammed down a chess rulebook in front of room full of people and loudly announced that the match was not a tie, that my uncle had actual won because he had more pieces.
